zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

headline: Uneven week, sharpening edge: the canyon bite is following the color break
subhead: Spencer and Norfolk producing when boats find the temperature seam; Lindenkohl and Poor Man's still sorting themselves out.
body_markdown:
Call it a C-plus week with an A finish for the boats that ran the right numbers. The canyon bite has been patchy canyon to canyon, and that's exactly what you'd expect this time of September, when the warm water mass that's been sitting out there all month starts getting squeezed by cooler shelf water pushing off the beach. We flagged this pattern last week and the week before — said the chlorophyll boundary overlapping the sharpening SST edge would keep concentrating bait and predators tight, and that's precisely what's playing out. The problem for a lot of boats isn't that the fish left. It's that the edge moved, and a chunk of the fleet ran the wrong canyon on the wrong day.

Spencer has been the most consistent stop this week, with the break sitting close enough to the shelf that boats running out of Ocean City could reach good color without burning half a tank getting there. Norfolk has fished well in stretches too, particularly when the warm filament pushed south and tightened up against the canyon wall — that's classic late-summer-into-fall behavior for that piece of bottom, and it's kept a mixed bag of yellowfin and a few bigeye showing up on the night chunk. Lindenkohl and Poor Man's have been the tougher rooms. Reports out of both spots this week describe clean but relatively barren water on the troll — the kind of blue that looks perfect and produces nothing because the temperature seam simply wasn't sitting on top of the bottom structure that day.

The why here is straightforward. When the SST break and the chlorophyll line stack on top of each other, you get a real wall of bait — squid, flying fish, small mahi forage — getting pinned against the edge, and everything from yellowfin to white marlin sets up on it to feed. When those two signatures separate, even by a few miles, the fish go with the bait and the boat sitting on yesterday's number gets a whole lot of nothing. That's the read for the tougher canyons this week. It's not that the fish quit. It's that they moved with the groceries.

On the gear side, the yellowfin have been coming both on the troll and the chunk depending on the canyon. Spreader bars pulling green machines and cedar plugs off the corners have accounted for fish in the 25 to 45-pound range along Spencer's edge, with the better morning bite running early before the wind fills in and chops the surface. Once the troll shuts down mid-morning, boats have been switching over to butterfish chunks on 50-pound fluorocarbon leaders, letting the chunk line drift back naturally with no weight, and picking away at yellowfin holding under the slick. That same chunk program at night has been the play for bigeye off Norfolk — small chunks of butterfish or sardine on a slow bump-and-drop through 300 to 500 feet of water, patience required, because the bites have been more about timing than volume this week.

White marlin have shown in ones and twos off both Spencer and Norfolk, mostly teased up on naked ballyhoo behind dredge teasers and pitched with a rigged ballyhoo or a Bonita strip once they commit. Nothing like a wide-open marlin bite, but enough activity along the temperature seam to keep the pitch rod rigged and ready on every troll spread run. Wahoo have been the wildcard — a handful of fish taken on high-speed presentations, Ilanders and cedar plugs run through the color change at 12 to 15 knots, mostly incidental to the tuna troll rather than a dedicated program, which tells you the wahoo push hasn't fully committed yet this far south. Mahi have been scattered around any floating structure or weed line that's held together, small fish mostly, worth a stop but not worth building a whole day around.

Looking at the next few days, the smart move is chasing the edge, not the canyon name. If the warm filament holds its position the way it has, Spencer and Norfolk stay the higher-percentage runs, with Norfolk carrying the better bigeye potential once the sun goes down. If that filament pushes further south or the shelf water intrudes harder from the north, watch for Lindenkohl and Poor Man's to come back into play fast — that's how this pattern has worked all month, one canyon goes quiet while the seam sets up better two canyons over. Check the latest water color and temp break before committing fuel, because the difference between a good trip and a long ride this week has been measured in a few miles, not a few knots of wind. The days are shortening and the water's starting its seasonal slide, which typically tightens these breaks up even more through the rest of September — worth being ready to jump canyons on short notice rather than marrying one spot out of habit.
